title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Jacksonville, FL: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Jacksonville ship repair, port, mill and bridge workers: code choice, Part B sites and eligibility for veterans. Get a quote.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Jacksonville: Six Days to Prepare First Coast Welders and Inspectors
html:
Jacksonville sits where the St. Johns River meets the Atlantic, and that geography explains most of its welding work: Navy ships, port cranes and terminals, river bridges, paper mills on the waterways, power plants and a rail network that fans out across the South-East. People who weld, fit, inspect or engineer in that economy often reach a point where a supervisor, a contract or a customer asks for the AWS Certified Welding Inspector credential. Atlantis NDT's six-day (6-day) exam-preparation course is built for that moment. North Florida candidates can follow it online around their shifts, and employers can bring the six days to their own yard, mill or shop for several people. The credential is awarded by AWS, which also sets the eligibility rules and runs each part of the examination; Atlantis's role ends at preparation. Send a Jacksonville enquiry to get a quote.

Four common routes into welding inspection on the First Coast

Most Jacksonville CWI candidates arrive from one of four directions, and each brings different strengths and gaps to the exam.

  1. Ship repair welders and fitters. Years of repair work on steel and aluminum hulls, decks and piping teach hands-on judgment, but repair crews often work to drawings and work packages rather than reading code books directly. Part C, the open-book code part, is usually where they need the most practice.
  2. Navy and military veterans. The two large Navy installations here, Naval Station Mayport and Naval Air Station Jacksonville, mean many people leave the service locally with hull maintenance, welding or quality assurance backgrounds. AWS asks for welding-related experience that can be documented, so collecting evaluations, training records and supervisor contacts before separation saves time later.
  3. Industrial maintenance technicians. Mill and power plant maintenance welders know repair procedures, preheat and difficult positions well, and they often have strong pipe skills. They tend to find the terminology and welding symbols in Part A the least familiar ground.
  4. Construction and fabrication QC staff. People already checking structural steel, stairs, rails or crane runways for a fabricator or testing laboratory usually know D1.1 in practice and need structure and timed practice more than new knowledge.

The six-day outline is the same for all four, but knowing which group you fall into tells you where to spend your study hours.

Navy ship repair: where a CWI fits and where it does not

Ship repair on Navy surface combatants is run under Navy contracts and Navy technical requirements, with their own welding and inspection standards and their own qualification rules for inspectors. A CWI does not automatically meet those requirements, and on some Navy work the contract names a different qualification entirely. So why do ship repair people around Mayport still pursue the CWI? Because shipyards and their subcontractors also do commercial vessel work, shore structures, cranes and fabrication jobs where the CWI is exactly what is asked for, and because the credential is portable when someone moves from a yard into construction, pipelines or plant inspection.

The honest advice for a Jacksonville ship repair worker is this: if your career will stay inside Navy repair, find out from your employer which inspector qualifications its contracts specify. If you want flexibility across industries, the CWI is the broadest welding inspection credential in the United States. For the NDT methods used on hull and piping repairs, see ultrasonic testing in marine work and magnetic particle testing in marine work.

JAXPORT terminals, cranes and vehicle-handling berths

The Jacksonville Port Authority runs container and vehicle terminals on the St. Johns, including Blount Island and Dames Point, and the port is a major gateway for imported and exported vehicles. Terminal work generates steady welding: ship-to-shore crane repairs and rail modifications, fender and bollard replacement, ramps, steel sheet pile and pile cap connections, and the steel structures of warehouses and processing buildings behind the docks. Much of that is structural steel welded to AWS D1.1, while crane manufacturers and owners may impose their own specifications on crane structures.

Inspectors on port projects deal with salt air, corrosion on old steel being repaired, and welding over existing members whose material is not well documented. That makes the Part A topics on base metal identification, preheat for unknown carbon content and the causes of cracking unusually practical. Crane and lifting equipment owners often add magnetic particle testing of critical welds; magnetic particle inspection of lifting equipment explains that test.

River bridges and moveable spans

Jacksonville is divided by a wide river, so its downtown is tied together by large bridges, including steel spans and a vertical-lift bridge, with further crossings along the river and to the beaches. Maintenance, rehabilitation and replacement of those structures, and of the many smaller bridges across north-east Florida, rely on bridge fabricators, repair contractors and inspection consultants. Steel bridge members are welded under AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code; its 2020 edition, fracture-critical clause and all, is one of the Part C books on the AWS list. If bridge steel is your trade, prepare with D1.5 instead of the structural code, and read the D1.5 overview for its main differences.

Moveable bridges add machinery: trunnions, racks, counterweight framing and lift towers, where welded repairs sit next to machined parts and inspectors coordinate closely with mechanical engineers. On those jobs a welding inspector's grasp of distortion, heat input and residual stress, all Fundamentals topics, has direct consequences for whether a span keeps operating smoothly.

Paper mills, power plants and rail shops

North-east Florida has long been paper mill country, and the region's power stations and industrial plants add to the steady maintenance welding market. Florida State College at Jacksonville describes its welding certificate as preparing students for careers in shipbuilding, paper mills and power plants, which is a fair summary of where local welders find work. Mill and plant work leans heavily on piping: steam, condensate, chemical recovery and process lines, with repairs made during short outages. Power piping is built to ASME B31.1, and process piping to ASME B31.3; both are Part C options in their 2024 editions. A maintenance welder who plans to stay in plant work should consider one of those books rather than D1.1. The B31.3 summary and ultrasonic testing in power generation explain how piping welds are usually examined.

Jacksonville is also a rail city, with a Class I railroad headquartered downtown and repair shops and yards across the region. Freight car and locomotive repair involves welding under railroad industry rules, and inspectors in that world benefit from the same fundamentals: discontinuities, fatigue cracking at weld toes, and the limits of visual inspection on parts that see cyclic loads. Magnetic particle testing in rail work covers the crack detection that often follows a visual check.

Where Jacksonville candidates sit the CWI exam

All three parts need a score of at least 72 percent, and they are taken in two different kinds of place:

Exam partFormatWhere it is taken
Part A, Fundamentals150 questions, computer-basedPrometric proctored test center, booked after AWS confirms your application
Part B, Practical46 questions with hands-on tasks using AWS-supplied equipmentAWS seminar locations only, on fixed dates
Part C, Code Book50 to 65 questions, open book, computer-basedPrometric proctored test center

The November 2026 AWS list of seminar and practical exam sites does not include Jacksonville. The nearest listed locations for a First Coast candidate are Tampa, Kennesaw in metro Atlanta, and Miami. Pick the one whose dates suit you, remember that AWS sets the US application deadline about six weeks before each Part B date, and do not book travel until your AWS confirmation letter arrives. Prepare for Part B with that trip in mind: arriving rested and familiar with the gauges counts for a lot. Pages for those markets: CWI exam prep in Tampa, CWI exam prep in Atlanta and CWI exam prep in Miami.

Local welding programs and the AWS North Florida Section

Two places in the city teach welding to the standard that leads toward inspection careers. Florida State College at Jacksonville offers a Welding Technology career certificate at its Downtown Campus, covering stick welding on plate and pipe and gas tungsten arc welding on steel, stainless steel and aluminum, with training toward the AWS 3G test series. Tulsa Welding School runs a Jacksonville campus on Southside Boulevard with a professional welder program. Trade and vocational coursework like this appears on the AWS eligibility table, where it cuts the experience requirement from five years for a high school graduate to four, so keep your certificates and transcripts.

The American Welding Society's North Florida Section, part of District 5, is the regional chapter for this part of the state. Its meetings and events connect working inspectors, welding instructors and employers, and they are a practical place to hear which code books local companies favor, to find study partners heading to the same Part B date, and to meet people who can later confirm your work history for AWS.

How the six days run for a Jacksonville candidate or employer

The course keeps a fixed order of six blocks. It opens with two fundamentals days: welding processes, AWS terminology, joint geometry and welding symbols first, then metallurgy, mechanical testing, discontinuities and their causes, NDT methods, safety and the inspector's responsibilities. Block three is hands-on readiness for Part B: gauge handling, sizing fillets and grooves, judging profile, and checking a joint against a written specification and its qualification paperwork. The fourth works inside your chosen Part C code. The fifth is timed practice papers for all three parts, and the sixth targets the weak spots those papers reveal, plus exam logistics and an application checklist. The national CWI preparation page walks through each block in detail.

Remote learners receive a paced plan, the reading list, freshly written practice items and written instructor help on request. That suits ship repair and mill schedules, where twelve-hour shifts and outages make fixed class hours unrealistic. When a yard, terminal contractor, mill or fabricator wants a team ready together, those six days move onto its premises; on the practical day your people measure your weld samples with your gauges, which ties the preparation to the joints they inspect. Atlantis keeps no office or classroom in Jacksonville; it works from Houston and Hyderabad and travels to host sites when a group books on-site delivery. The practice questions are written fresh against the published topic list and never copied from AWS papers.

Eligibility and documents: what to gather first

AWS reviews eligibility before it confirms any exam. The required years of welding-related experience fall as education rises, from twelve years for someone with less than eighth-grade schooling, through nine with eighth grade and five with a high school diploma, down to a single year for a bachelor's in welding engineering or welding technology. You must also pass AWS's vision test. Veterans should translate military duties into plain descriptions of welding, fitting or weld quality work and attach supporting records; AWS is the only party that can decide whether specific experience counts, so ask it directly if you are unsure.

Candidates without enough years yet can look at the CAWI, AWS's associate-level inspector credential, which asks for less experience. The full set of rules is discussed in our CWI requirements guide, and the career step after CWI is covered in the Senior CWI pathway.

Request a Jacksonville quote

Tell us who needs preparation, how many people, each person's background (ship repair, mill, construction, military), the Part C code book each expects to use, and which Part B site and season you are targeting. Employers should also say where the six days would run. We reply within one business day. For exam and seminar charges, go straight to aws.org, where AWS keeps them current; the CWI budget planner helps you add travel to a Part B site. Start your Jacksonville request.

Many welding inspectors later add NDT method qualifications. For that side, Atlantis offers ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based NDT training; certification under that document comes from the employer's written practice, not from a course; see NDT training in Jacksonville, visual testing in Jacksonville and VT Level 1 training.

faq.q: Is there a CWI practical exam site in Jacksonville?
faq.a: Not on the AWS list as of November 2026. North Florida candidates usually look at Tampa, Kennesaw (metro Atlanta) or Miami. Check aws.org for current sites and dates.

faq.q: Can I take Parts A and C in Jacksonville?
faq.a: Parts A and C are computer-based exams given by Prometric at proctored test centers. Once AWS confirms your application, use Prometric's locator to find the nearest center.

faq.q: Does a CWI qualify me to inspect welds on Navy ship repair contracts?
faq.a: Not automatically. Navy repair work runs to Navy technical requirements, which may specify other inspector qualifications. Ask your employer which qualifications its contracts require.

faq.q: Can my military welding experience count toward CWI eligibility?
faq.a: It can if AWS accepts it as welding-related experience you can document. Gather evaluations, training records and supervisor contacts, and ask AWS directly about anything you are unsure of.

faq.q: Which Part C code suits paper mill or power plant maintenance work?
faq.a: Usually a piping code: ASME B31.1 for power piping or ASME B31.3 for process piping. Both are on the AWS list of Part C books.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis classroom in Jacksonville?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad. Jacksonville candidates study online, or an employer can host the six-day course at its own facility.

faq.q: Can a Jacksonville shipyard or contractor have the course at its site?
faq.a: Yes. The six days can be delivered for a group at the employer's facility, and practical exercises built around that firm's tools and real joints. Request a quote.

faq.q: Who certifies me as a CWI?
faq.a: AWS certifies CWIs after you meet its eligibility rules, pass the vision test and pass all three exam parts. Atlantis is not approved or endorsed by AWS and does not certify anyone.

faq.q: Do FSCJ or welding school certificates help with eligibility?
faq.a: Trade or vocational coursework counts on the AWS eligibility table and lowers the experience requirement compared with a high school diploma alone. AWS decides how a specific program is classified.
The AWS North Florida Section, part of District 5, is the chapter for north-east Florida.
